kurz: Why a change in the level of interest rates shifts property prices, equity valuations and the value of savings all at once.

bloecke.md:
Interest is the price of having money at your disposal today that belongs to someone else. Like other prices, it is made up of several components: compensation for the waiting time, a premium for the risk that the money will not be repaid, a premium for expected inflation and a margin for whoever handles the transaction.

That is why there are many different interest rates on the same day, and they lie far apart. The gaps between them provide information about maturities, about the credit quality of borrowers, that is, their creditworthiness, and about the expectations of market participants.

bloecke.md:
## Nominal and real

The first distinction is between the agreed interest rate and the interest actually earned in real terms. The nominal interest rate is written in the contract; the [[real interest rate]] is what remains after deducting inflation. German inflation was 2.9% in August 2026, and the ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September. The short-term real interest rate is therefore negative. So there is interest again, but no gain in purchasing power yet.

Strictly speaking, what counts is *expected* inflation and not past inflation. It cannot be observed, so the real interest rate is an estimate beforehand and only becomes a measurement in hindsight. The ECB projection of 10 September 2026 foresees inflation of 3.0% for 2026, 2.5% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028. Investors who lock in their money for ten years today are thus implicitly betting on such a development.

bloecke.erklaerung: Fisher equation. For small values, the approximation r = i − p is accurate enough. With double-digit inflation it deviates noticeably, giving a positive real interest rate that is too high and a negative one that is too low.

bloecke.md:
€10,000 sits in an instant-access savings account at 2.0% (banks rarely pass on the deposit facility rate in full), and inflation is a constant 2.9%.

- After ten years the balance is €12,190.
- Its purchasing power corresponds to €9,159 in today's money.

In nominal terms that is a gain of 22%, in real terms a loss of 8%. The illustrative calculation with constant rates only shows the direction.

bloecke.titel: Nominal and real yield on ten-year Bunds
bloecke.unter: Annual averages of the nominal yield and of the real yield, which is calculated using the Fisher equation with the inflation of the same year (ex post).

bloecke.md:
Averaged over the years 1970 to 2025, the ten-year German federal bond (Bund) returned 2.3% in real terms. The average covers two very different phases: 1980 to 1999 at a real 4.3% a year and 2010 to 2021 at minus 0.6%. The real yield was negative in nine of 56 years, and all nine lie after 2011.

The nominal figures alone easily lead to false conclusions. In 1974 a coupon of over 10% was considered very attractive, but 3.3% remained in real terms. In 2021 the same bond yielded minus 0.37%, in real terms minus 3.4%. After 2022 (minus 5.4%), that is the second-worst year in the series.

bloecke.titel: The natural rate of interest r*
bloecke.md:
Underlying the structure of interest rates is a quantity that cannot be measured: the natural or neutral rate of interest, called r* in the literature. It means the real interest rate at which an economy is working at full capacity without generating price pressure, and at which monetary policy neither brakes nor stimulates. Knut Wicksell formulated the idea at the end of the 19th century. Today r* is estimated with statistical filters from growth, inflation and interest rates; a well-known method is that of Laubach and Williams.

The estimates have fallen over decades, which is attributed to demographics, weak productivity and high saving. More important than the individual figure is that r* is a model result with a wide band of uncertainty. The margin of error of the estimate can be larger than the rate step being argued about.

## Short-term and long-term rates

The second distinction concerns maturity. The [[yield curve]] shows, for borrowers of the same credit quality, here the German federal government, the yield as a function of remaining maturity. According to the expectations theory, the ten-year yield roughly equals the average of the short-term rates expected over the next ten years. In addition, there is a [[term premium]] as compensation for the investor committing for so long. Central banks therefore set only the shortest rate; the market forms all the others. This is clearly visible in 2026, as ten-year yields have risen more than key interest rates.

bloecke.unter: Normal upward-sloping curve with a spread of 59 basis points between two-year and thirty-year maturities; the long commitment is moderately rewarded.

bloecke.titel: Steepness of the yield curve (ten minus two years)
bloecke.unter: Year-end levels, for 2026 the level on 18 September; negative values mean an inverted curve, in which long maturities yield less than short ones.

bloecke.md:
An inverted curve typically arises when the central bank raises short-term rates sharply to fight inflation, while the market is already pricing in rate cuts at the long end because it expects the economy to cool. That is why it is regarded as a recession signal.

In the USA the curve has been inverted in around 120 of 812 months since 1959, about 15% of the time. Every US recession since 1966 was preceded by an inversion, with a lead time of 6 to 18 months. Conversely, however, not every inversion was followed by a recession. The inversion from November 2022 to November 2024 lasted 25 months, making it the longest in the series. By September 2026 it had not been followed by an officially dated recession, which made it the biggest false alarm in the history of the indicator. In Germany the curve was inverted for 459 trading days, followed by stagnation but no deep recession. The New York Fed's model, which evaluates this US curve, puts the probability of a recession in the following year at just under 14% in late summer 2026. The inversion is thus a well-founded warning signal, but a recession does not necessarily follow it.

## Discounting and valuation

Every asset that promises future payments is worth today what those payments are worth when discounted to the present day. The discounting is done with the interest rate. This means the interest rate influences the prices of all assets, because it is in the denominator of every valuation, whether of a bond, a property, a company or a pension commitment.

bloecke.erklaerung: The interest factor is raised to the power of the number of years. Besides its size, the effect of a change in interest rates therefore depends above all on how far in the future the payment lies.
bloecke.beispiel: €100 in 30 years is worth €86.10 today at 0.5% interest, and only €35.63 at 3.5%.

bloecke.titel: Present value of a future payment of €100

bloecke.md: In the middle column the values fall noticeably, in the right-hand column very sharply. This explains why changes in interest rates hit growth companies, very long-dated bonds and infrastructure projects harder than utilities, short-dated bonds and businesses that are already making money today. What matters, then, is when the bulk of the payments falls, regardless of the sector.

bloecke.titel: Valuation at two interest rate levels
bloecke.md:
A simplified model sets the value of a perpetually growing payment at the payment divided by (discount rate minus growth rate). The assumptions are a payout of €3 per share, 2% growth and a risk premium of 5 percentage points over the Bund yield.

- Bund yield −0.5% (2020 annual average), discount rate 4.5% → 3 / (0.045 − 0.02) = €120.00
- Bund yield 3.5% (September 2026), discount rate 8.5% → 3 / (0.085 − 0.02) = €46.15

The second value is just over 60% below the first, even though nothing has changed at the company. In reality, the risk premium moves too, profits grow or collapse, and no company pays out evenly for ever. The calculation therefore only shows the direction and the order of magnitude.

## Interest rates in mortgage financing

Private individuals feel interest rates most clearly with the largest sum of their lives: financing a property. An annuity, that is, a constant instalment, consists of interest and repayment. As long as the instalment is fixed, the more of it goes on interest, the less is left for repayment. With a loan of €400,000, a borrowing rate of 3.97% and an initial repayment rate of 2%, the instalment is €23,880 a year, just under €1,990 a month. Of this, €15,880 goes to the bank in the first year and only €8,000 into repayment. The reverse calculation shows what loan a fixed monthly instalment can support, and thus what purchase prices households can afford across the whole property market.

bloecke.titel: Loan amount for a monthly instalment of €1,000
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with an initial repayment rate of 2%, loan = annual instalment / (borrowing rate + repayment rate); the borrowing rate of 3.97% reflects market conditions in September 2026.

bloecke.md: With the mortgage rates of 2026, the same household can borrow only half as much for the same instalment as with the mortgage rates of the zero-interest years. Purchase prices therefore do not automatically fall to the same extent, because location, supply and construction costs continue to play a role. The gap does, however, put pressure on prices, equity ratios and construction volumes.

bloecke.titel: Key interest rate, mortgage rate and instant-access savings
bloecke.md: The ECB deposit facility rate is an overnight rate for banks. Mortgage rates are based on the capital market (Pfandbrief covered bonds and Bunds) and can rise while the central bank is cutting. Interest on deposits does not follow the key interest rate evenly either. Rising key interest rates reach instant-access savings accounts with a delay and only partly, whereas falling ones arrive quickly. Interest rate news from Frankfurt therefore cannot be transferred one for one to your account or loan agreement.

## The effect of interest rates on the government budget

For the state, the largest debtor in the country, a change in interest rates takes effect most slowly. A higher market rate only affects the part of the debt that is currently being newly issued or refinanced. The average interest rate on a stock of debt built up over decades therefore only changes over the course of years. A turn in the interest rate cycle thus initially seems to have no consequences for public budgets, and the pressure to adjust is pushed into the future.

## The zero interest rate phase in historical comparison

The years in which money cost nothing were an exception. The ECB deposit facility rate was negative from June 2014 to July 2022 and stood at minus 0.50% from September 2019. For eight years, banks paid to hold money at the central bank. On 9 March 2020 the ten-year Bund yielded minus 0.85%, the lowest daily value in the Bundesbank series since 1997. The US key interest rate was practically zero from December 2008 to December 2015 and again from March 2020 to March 2022, around nine of eighteen years in total.

Viewed over a longer period, a different picture emerges. In 1974 Bunds yielded an annual average of 10.44%, and in 1981 10.13%. Both extremes follow the same mechanism, just with different inflation and different expectations.

An interest rate below zero means that the creditor pays for leaving their money with someone else. Economically, this is only possible as long as the alternative is more expensive. Cash earns 0%, but it involves storage, insurance and transport costs and is impractical for amounts in the billions. These costs determine the effective lower bound, a fuzzy threshold slightly below zero.

Banks initially passed the burden on only to large customers. When they later also charged retail customers custody fees (Verwahrentgelte), the issue was argued before German courts. After the turn in the interest rate cycle in 2022, most banks stopped charging custody fees. On 4 February 2025 the Federal Court of Justice (BGH) declared the clauses at issue for current accounts, instant-access savings accounts and savings accounts invalid (XI ZR 61/23 and others). During the negative interest rate phase, buyers of bonds with negative yields rarely acted in the hope of a return. They mostly bought because of regulatory requirements, as insurance against a worse scenario or in the expectation of being able to sell the bonds on at a price gain.

Interest is the price of time and therefore the denominator of every valuation. If it rises, the value of everything whose returns lie in the future falls: bond prices, property prices and the valuations of companies whose profits lie far ahead. This follows mathematically from discounting, regardless of market sentiment.

1. Mentally subtract the current inflation rate from every interest rate offer.
2. For every fixed rate, clarify the period it applies to and what happens afterwards. This applies to investments and loans alike.
3. When looking at interest rate forecasts, bear in mind that the central bank only sets the short end. Short-term and long-term rates can move in opposite directions, as in 2025, when the ECB cut its key interest rates and the yields on ten-year Bunds rose.

mitnehmen: The nominal interest rate is in the contract, while the real interest rate determines purchasing power; a deposit facility rate of 2.50% with inflation of 2.9% gives minus 0.4% in real terms.
Central banks set the shortest interest rate; the market forms the yields on long-term bonds from expectations about inflation, growth and risk.
Historically, an inverted yield curve has preceded every US recession, but not every inversion has been followed by a recession; the 2022 to 2024 inversion was the biggest false alarm so far.
Because discounting raises the interest factor to the power of the number of years, changes in interest rates hit distant payments much harder than near ones.
The nine of 56 years with a negative real bond yield all lie after 2011; zero interest rates were an exceptional phase.

begriffe.text: The nominal interest rate adjusted for (expected) inflation. Exactly, it is (1+i)/(1+p) − 1, approximately i − p. It determines purchasing power and can be negative even though the contractual interest rate is positive.
Chart of yields of the same credit quality by remaining maturity. It normally slopes upwards. In times of uncertainty it is flat, and it is inverted when short-term rates are above long-term ones.
The premium that investors demand for tying up capital for longer. Together with the expected short-term rates, it explains the level of long-term yields.
The value today of a future payment, that is, the payment divided by (1 + discount rate) to the power of the number of years. It is the basis of every valuation of bonds, property and companies.
The real interest rate at which the economy is working at full capacity without generating price pressure. It cannot be observed and is estimated with a considerable band of uncertainty.
